clue.text: Wild flower seen in another place?

definitions.meaning: a name for the wild arum or cuckoo-pint, a hedgerow plant
'another place' is how MPs in the Commons refer to the House of Lords, whose members are peers and peeresses

explanation.walkthrough: In Westminster custom each House calls the other 'another place', so the members seen there are its titled peers.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a folk name for the arum plant, and the titled members of Britain's upper chamber.

clue.text: Putting baby in cot, one may fail one's colleagues

definitions.meaning: lowering the drop-side rail of a cot so the infant can be placed inside

explanation.walkthrough: The literal sense is a parent lowering the cot rail; the idiom is letting one's team down.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a literal lowering of a cot's rail, and the idiom for disappointing teammates.

clue.text: Core of Brie, and a large helping of cottage cheese

indicators.note: the core of a word is its middle, so the central letters of Brie are taken
a large helping is most of the word, so the final pair of letters of cottage is dropped

explanation.surface: A cheeseboard serving of the inside of a Brie and plenty of cottage cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Core of' takes RI from the middle of Brie; 'a large helping of' leaves COTTA from cottage once GE is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Ricotta is a soft Italian whey cheese, so it is an example of a cheese.

clue.text: Alexander's son, Andrew

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for son in genealogies
Andy is the familiar short form of the name Andrew

explanation.surface: A family tree notes that Alexander has a boy called Andrew.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Alexander is 'has', linking the definition to the wordplay; it looks like a possessive about Alexander's child.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandy is a common Scottish pet form of the given name, so it stands for that name.

clue.text: The Scrubs, perhaps

parts.note: Wormwood Scrubs is a London prison, and 'The Scrubs' is its familiar label; a prison is slang 'nick', so this is the nick's informal title

explanation.walkthrough: Wormwood Scrubs is a well-known London jail; 'nick' is British slang for a prison, so a jail's pet name is a 'nick name'.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal pet title for something, here an affectionate label for a famous jail.

clue.text: See, in the limelight, a girl described by Nabokov

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
lit up, as by a spotlight on stage

explanation.surface: A critic notes a young girl in the spotlight in a Nabokov novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Nabokov's novel is a twelve-year-old girl, so she is the girl he wrote about.

clue.text: Dissolute young girl, upper-class, longed to go outside

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, a young society girl

indicators.note: the longing word goes round the upper-class letter, enclosing it

parts.note: ached, as in yearned
U is the abbreviation for upper-class usage

explanation.surface: A dissolute young society girl, posh and pining, wants to get out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'young girl' is the society debutante, and 'upper-class' uses the old U versus non-U label for posh speech; 'to go outside' wraps the longing word round that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A debauched person has given up morals for pleasure, the same as a dissolute one.

clue.text: Where Paulette has hidden symbol of American rank

indicators.note: the run of letters lies concealed inside the two words where and Paulette

explanation.surface: A woman named Paulette has tucked away a US military badge somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: The American spelling has one T, matching the run inside 'Where Paulette'.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoulder ornament on a uniform marks an officer's grade, and this single-T form is the US spelling.

clue.text: Unfaithful wife they called arty-crafty

indicators.note: crafty suggests cunning reworking, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: People dismissed the adulterous wife as arty-crafty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arty-crafty' looks like one adjective, but 'arty' is fodder and 'crafty' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence's heroine Constance, Lady Chatterley, betrays her husband with the gamekeeper.

clue.text: Catch line that's thrown, requiring special skill

indicators.note: thrown means tossed about or disordered, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Angling with a cast line demands expertise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'thrown' looks like a cast fishing line, but it signals an anagram of CATCH and LINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical work calls for specialist know-how, so it requires particular skill.

clue.text: Master has scholar, somewhat pale, kept in

indicators.note: the pale word is held inside the scholar's letters

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a scholar
wan means rather pale, sickly-looking

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster has a slightly pallid student kept in detention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat pale' looks like a description of the scholar, but it is a separate piece; 'kept in' puts it inside the degree letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Bwana is a Swahili form of address meaning master or boss, used in colonial East Africa.

clue.text: In good time, showing eagerness

indicators.note: the time letter goes inside the word for good

parts.note: holy means virtuous, saintly

explanation.surface: Arriving promptly shows keenness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In good time' reads as 'promptly', but it is T put inside HOLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something hotly means doing it with passion and keenness, as in a hotly contested race.

clue.text: Verdict letting you loose, free, finally released

indicators.note: set loose means freed and scattered, so the letters are rearranged
released means let go, so that letter is removed
finally points to the last letter of free

explanation.surface: The jury's decision sets the defendant free, at last released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives E from free; 'released' takes it out of LETTING, leaving LTTING; 'loose' then rearranges LTTING and YOU.
explanation.definitionFit: Acquittal is the court's decision that the accused did not commit the crime, a type of verdict.

clue.text: I don't know what suspicious police might do

definitions.meaning: a shrugging colloquial reply meaning I have no idea
officers who suspect someone could frisk the speaker

explanation.walkthrough: The informal shrug 'no idea' also reads literally as an invitation to be frisked.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: a casual phrase of ignorance, and a literal request for a frisk by officers.

clue.text: Domestic pets always quarrelling

definitions.meaning: a feline and a canine, the two commonest household animals
a fight that is constant and bitter, like the proverbial enmity of those two animals

explanation.walkthrough: Note that the enumeration is hyphenated (3-3-3): the phrase works as an adjective, as in a constant fight.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: the two common household animals, and an adjective for incessant bickering.

clue.text: Roof covering which church put on

indicators.note: the church letters are added onto the end of the other word

parts.note: that and which are interchangeable relative pronouns

explanation.surface: Which church's roof did they cover in straw?
explanation.definitionFit: Thatch is straw or reed laid as a roofing material, so it covers a roof.

clue.text: Shopping centre making a hit in the 60s

definitions.meaning: the business and retail district of a town
Petula Clark's 1964 chart single of that title

explanation.walkthrough: Petula Clark's song was a transatlantic number one in the mid-sixties; 'making' simply links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: an American term for the commercial core of a town, and a famous sixties pop song.

clue.text: Departs this world in want

parts.note: D is the timetable abbreviation for departs
the earth is the world we live on

explanation.surface: Someone leaves this life in poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' joins wordplay to definition; 'want' is a noun meaning lack, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dearth is a scarcity or shortage, which is what want means as a noun.

clue.text: One who may become married

indicators.note: the letters of the word can be turned into another word, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suitor is someone who might end up wed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition (a suitor may end up wed) and the wordplay: 'may become' rearranges MARRIED.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitor or devotee courting someone is a would-be partner who may eventually wed.

clue.text: Loss of nerve as a result of paddling in winter ?

definitions.meaning: the idiom for last-minute anxiety that makes someone back out

definitions.text: as a result of paddling in winter ?
definitions.meaning: literally, wading in chilly water leaves the toes chilled

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom for losing courage is read literally as chilled toes after a winter paddle.
explanation.definitionFit: Double definition: the idiom for losing courage before a commitment, and literal chilled toes.

clue.text: Sparse lot of soldiers supporting English queen

indicators.note: in a down entry the supporting pieces sit underneath the English letter

parts.note: lean means thin, meagre
OR, other ranks, are the soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: A thin troop of soldiers holds up England's queen.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supporting' means coming below, so the thin word and the soldiers sit under the English letter; 'lot of soldiers' is the army's other ranks.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor of Aquitaine and Eleanor of Castile were both queens of England.

clue.text: Bill has small amount added — it could be grave

parts.note: AC is the abbreviation for account, a bill
a cent is a tiny sum of money

explanation.surface: A bill with a little extra tacked on might be a serious matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grave' looks like serious, but the grave is a mark over a letter, as in à.
explanation.definitionFit: The grave is one kind of diacritic mark, so it is an example of this written sign.

clue.text: West Indian 'fellow grabs a taxi, not black

indicators.note: the fellow's letters seize the taxi word, holding it inside

parts.note: a don is a college fellow

indicators.note: not means without, so the black letter is removed

parts.note: a minicab is a type of taxi
B is the pencil-grading abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: A Caribbean man grabs a cab, though not one in a black livery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' takes the black letter from the taxi, and 'grabs' sets what is left inside the college fellow; the opening quote mark is a stray from the printed page.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Dominica or the Dominican Republic is from the West Indies.

clue.text: Bit of dessert before church

indicators.note: the dessert word comes first, ahead of the church letters

parts.note: a pie is a pudding course
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A slice of pudding eaten before the Sunday service.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is a bit or portion of something, synonyms in the sense of a fragment.

clue.text: So that is fundamental

annotationWithheld.why: So that is fundamental (5) for PRIME: scan agrees; 'that is' suggests IE but no reading of 'So' supplies P, R and M around it, so no honest parse found

clue.text: Everyone spun round, hearing it

indicators.note: the word for spun round is said aloud, signalling a homophone

parts.note: whirled means rotated rapidly

explanation.surface: Everybody twirled about at the sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hearing it' tells the solver to use the sound of WHIRLED.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiomatically the whole world means all people, as in the world and his wife.

clue.text: Feeling too menial, debased

indicators.note: debased means corrupted, so the letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone feels far too lowly and degraded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feeling' is an adjective here, as in a feeling heart.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, feeling means sensitive and moved by sentiment, the same as passionate or tearful.

clue.text: At the crack of dawn, economist acquires article at great cost

parts.note: John Bright was a Victorian campaigner for free trade and repeal of the Corn Laws
an is the indefinite article
dearly means at high price

explanation.surface: Early in the morning an economist picks up an expensive item.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bright, a nineteenth-century British radical, championed free-trade economics; 'acquires' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means very early in the morning, cheerfully at daybreak.
